{{Short description|Italian mathematician and astronomer}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2024}}
[[File:Jean de Castillon.png|thumb|Castillon: ''Observations sur le livre intitulé Systême de la nature'' (1771)]]
'''Giovanni Francesco Mauro Melchiorre Salvemini di Castiglione''' {{post-nominal styles|FRS|country=GBR}} (15 January 1708 in [[Castiglion Fibocchi|Castiglione del Valdarno]] – 11 October 1791 in [[Berlin]])<ref name="Spiess">{{NDB|3|174|174|Castillon, Jean|Spiess, Otto |104342803}}</ref> was an [[Italians|Italian]] [[mathematician]] and [[astronomer]].

==Life==
Salvemini was born on 15 January 1708 in [[Castiglion Fibocchi|Castiglione del Valdarno]] (currently in the [[province of Arezzo]]), [[Grand Duchy of Tuscany]].<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia|title=Castiglióne, Giovanni Francesco Salvemini detto |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia Online |language=it |publisher=Treccani |url=http://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/giovanni-francesco-salvemini-detto-castiglione/ }}</ref> His father, Giuseppe Salvemini of [[Castiglion Fiorentino]], was a diplomat and jurist, and an ambassador for the Grand Duchy.<ref name="Guicciardini">{{Cite encyclopedia|editor-last=Guicciardini |editor-first=Niccolò |year=2017 |title=Salvemini, Giovanni Francesco |encyclopedia=Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani |volume=89 |language=it |url=http://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/giovanni-francesco-salvemini_(Dizionario-Biografico) }}</ref>  His mother was Maria Maddalena Lucia Braccesi whose family came from Pisa.<ref name="Guicciardini" /><ref name="St-Andrews-bio">{{Cite web|last1=O'Connor |first1=J. J. |last2=Robertson |first2=E. F. |year=2009 |title=Johann Francesco Melchiore Salvemini Castillon |work=Biographies |publisher=[[University of St Andrews]] |location=[[Fife, Scotland]] |url=http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Biographies/Castillon.html }}</ref> Salvemini was home schooled by tutors and then attended a seminary in [[Florence]].<ref name="Guicciardini" />

He graduated from the [[University of Pisa]] where he studied law and mathematics, earning a doctorate on 3 March 1730.<ref name="Guicciardini" /> On 8 January 1732 he was appointed as a sub-chancellor at the Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore, for a five-year term. His religious views having evolved, he left his job and fled the [[Inquisition]] to Switzerland in 1736.<ref>{{Cite book|editor1-last=Laursen |editor1-first=John Christian |editor2-last=Blom |editor2-first=H. W. |editor3-last=Simonutti |editor3-first=Luisa |year=2007 |title=Monarchisms in the Age of Enlightenment: Liberty, patriotism, and the common good |publisher=University of Toronto Press |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=kvPMjYbAreYC&pg=PA268 268] |isbn=978-0-8020-9177-2 }}</ref> On 16 April 1737, he formally enrolled in the [[Calvinism|Calvinist faith]] in [[Geneva]].<ref name="Guicciardini" />

He settled in [[Vevey]] near [[Lausanne]], where in August 1737 he received an appointment as the principal at the school. He was known in French as '''Jean de Castillon'''. He taught there until 1748 when he was dismissed due in part to his harsh teaching methods.<ref name="Guicciardini" /> Unable to find employment in Switzerland, in 1751 he obtained a job teaching mathematics and astronomy at the [[University of Utrecht]] where he began work on a second doctorate, which he received in 1754 under the name '''Johann Castillon'''. He was made a professor of mathematics and philosophy there the following year, and served as the [[Rector (academia)|rector]] there from 1758 to 1759.<ref name="St-Andrews-bio" />

In 1763, [[Frederick the Great]] invited Salvemini to [[Berlin]] to teach mathematics to Prussian artillery officers.<ref name="Spiess"/><ref>Later, after his death, this became the Unified Artillery and Engineering School ([[:de:Vereinigte Artillerie- und Ingenieurschule]]) at [[Charlottenburg]]. {{Cite dictionary|title=Vereinigte Artillerie- und Ingenieurschule |dictionary=Meyers Großes Konversations-Lexikon |location=Leipzig |year=1909 |volume=20 |page=48 |url=http://www.zeno.org/Meyers-1905/A/Vereinigte+Artillerie-+und+Ingenieurschule }}</ref> Although he had been a [[corresponding member]] since 1755, in 1764 he was elected a full member of the [[Prussian Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="Spiess"/> That same year Salvemini moved to Berlin.<ref name="Spiess"/> In 1765, he received the position of First Astronomer ("Royal Astronomer") at the [[Berlin Observatory]].<ref name="St-Andrews-bio" /> He remained in Berlin for the rest of his life.<ref name="St-Andrews-bio" /> Although he had a stroke in November 1787, he remained lucid and continued his work until his death.<ref name="Spiess"/>

===Personal life===
In 1745, he married Elizabeth du Fresne with whom he had three children, the only surviving child was Maximilian Friedrich Gustav Adolf Salvemini (see below). In 1757, Elizabeth died, and he married Madeleine Ravené in November 1759 in the Walloon Church of Amsterdam.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://archief.amsterdam/indexen/deeds/06b34db0-b3a8-4689-ab5c-f78b7f5dddf1|title=Marriage record of Jean Castillion and Magdelaine Ravené |work=Ondertrouwregister|publisher=Gemeente Amsterdam Stadsarchief|access-date=2025-08-19}}</ref> He met the Scottish diarist [[James Boswell]] in both Utrecht and Berlin, with Boswell recording several anecdotes and conversations.<ref name="St-Andrews-bio" />

His son [[Frederick Salvemini de Castillon]] (1747-1814) also became a member  [[Prussian Academy of Sciences|Berlin Academy]] and was a writer for ''[[Encyclopédie|Diderot's Encyclopédie]]''.<ref>{{Cite magazine|title=The Freemason's Lexicon: Von Castillon Frederick Gustav Adolph Maximilion |magazine=Freemasons' Quarterly Magazine (New Series) |location=London |year=1844 |page=415 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IfcDAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA415 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite encyclopedia|title=Castillon (Frédéric-Adolphe-Maximilien-Gustave de)|last=Fétis |first=François-Joseph |year=1875 |encyclopedia=Biographie universelle des musiciens et bibliographie générale de la musique |location=Paris |publisher=Firmin-Didot |volume=2 |page=208 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NE5DAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA208 }}</ref>

==Mathematics==
In 1745, he was elected to the [[Royal Society]]. In 1765, [[Frederick the Great]] appointed him "Astronomer Royal", of the Observatory of Berlin. He received additional honours from foreign academies, was appointed a member of the Academy of Bologna in 1768, the Academy of Mannheim in 1777, the Academy of Padua in 1784, and the Academy of Prague in 1785. Succeeding [[Joseph-Louis Lagrange]], he was appointed Director of the Mathematics Section of the [[Prussian Academy of Sciences|Berlin Academy]], a role he held until his death.<ref name="St-Andrews-bio" />

He studied [[conic section]]s, [[cubic equation]]s and problems of artillery. He is also known for solving the [[Cramer–Castillon problem]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Starck |first=Maurice |year=2002 |title=Castillon's problem |url=http://wwwedu.ge.ch/cptic/clubs/cabri/download/lettre96/Preuve_Starck.pdf |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110706232612/http://wwwedu.ge.ch/cptic/clubs/cabri/download/lettre96/Preuve_Starck.pdf |archivedate=6 July 2011 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Works==
* ''Discours sur l’origine de l’inégalité parmi les hommes. Pour servir de reponse au discours que M Rouseau'' (1756)
* ''Mémoire sur la règle de Cardan, et sur les equations cubique, avec Quelques Remarques sur les equations en général'' (1783)
* ''Examen philosophique de principes de quelque algebra'' 1790 and 1791 (memoirs)
